Focus: Intrinsic Valuation, DDM, DCF, DuPont (Random Subset)

The Philosophy of Valuation

  • Valuation: Art or Science?
    • Myths (Misconceptions)
      • "A valuation is an objective search for true value" (False: All are biased)
      • "A good valuation provides a precise estimate" (False: No precision)
      • "The more quantitative, the better" (False: Simpler is often better)
    • Approaches
      • Intrinsic Valuation
        • Fundamentals: Cash Flows, Growth, Risk
        • Assumption: Markets make mistakes that correct over time
      • Relative Valuation
        • Pricing based on "Comparables" (Peers)
        • Assumption: Markets are correct on average
    • The First Principle
      • Consistency Principle (Crucial!)
        • Match Cash Flows to Discount Rates
        • Equity Cash Flow $\to$ Cost of Equity ($r_e$)
        • Firm Cash Flow (Pre-debt) $\to$ Cost of Capital (WACC)
        • Trap: Never discount FCFF with $r_e$!

Intrinsic Valuation Models

  • Dividend Discount Models (DDM)
    • General Concept
      • Value = PV of expected future dividends
      • Origin: Stocks viewed as "Special Bonds"
    • Gordon Growth Model (Stable)
      • Formula: $P_0 = \frac{D_1}{k-g}$
      • Assumption: $k > g$ (Required)
      • Assumption: Stable Payout & Leverage
      • Case: Consolidated Edison (Utility)
    • Two-Stage Model (Growth)
      • Phase 1: High Growth
        • Explicitly forecast dividends year by year
        • Reason: $g$ is unstable or $> k$
      • Phase 2: Stable Growth
        • Calculate Horizon Value ($P_n$) using Gordon Model
        • Trap: $P_n$ is value at year $n$, discount back $n$ years!
    • Free Cash Flow (Advanced)
      • FCFE (Equity) vs. Dividend
      • Why FCFE? Companies (like Apple/Google) hoard cash/buybacks
      • Adjustment: Dividend + Share Repurchases

Analyzing Value Drivers (DuPont)

  • Where does Growth ($g$) come from?
    • The Formula
      • $g = \text{Retention Ratio (b)} \times ROE$
      • To grow, you must reinvest!
    • DuPont Decomposition of ROE
      • 1. Net Profit Margin
        • $\frac{\text{Net Income}}{\text{Sales}}$
        • Measures: Operating Efficiency / Pricing Power
        • Case: Maotai (High Margin)
      • 2. Asset Turnover
        • $\frac{\text{Sales}}{\text{Total Assets}}$
        • Measures: Asset Use Efficiency
        • Case: Walmart (High Turnover)
      • 3. Equity Multiplier
        • $\frac{\text{Total Assets}}{\text{Total Equity}}$
        • Measures: Financial Leverage
        • Trap: High ROE due to high leverage is risky!
        • Case: Zhong Lian (Margin dropped, Leverage rose)
    • Value Creation Condition
      • If $ROE > k$: Growth creates value
      • If $ROE < k$: Growth destroys value (Don't expand!)

Risk & Return (CAPM)

  • The Discount Rate ($k$)
    • Risk-Free Rate ($R_f$)
      • Proxy: 10-Year Treasury Bond Yield
      • Real Rate + Inflation Expectations
    • Equity Risk Premium ($R_m - R_f$)
      • Extra return demanded for holding stocks
      • Historical Avg: ~4.5% - 6%
    • Beta ($\beta$)
      • Measures: Systematic Risk
      • Slope of regression line (Asset vs Market)
      • $\beta > 1$: Aggressive (e.g. Tech, Banks)
      • $\beta < 1$: Defensive (e.g. Utilities like Con Ed)
  • Modern Portfolio Theory
    • Efficient Frontier
      • Driven by Correlation ($\rho < 1$)
      • Goal: Maximize Sharpe Ratio
  • APT (Arbitrage Pricing Theory) — L7
    • Market Model
      • $\tilde{r} = \alpha + \beta\tilde{R}_M + \tilde{\varepsilon}$
      • Market Model ≠ CAPM (statistical vs. equilibrium)
    • Variance Decomposition
      • Systematic: $\beta^2\sigma^2(R_M)$ — non-diversifiable
      • Non-systematic: $\sigma^2(\varepsilon)$ — diversifiable
      • $R^2$ = share of systematic variance
    • Multi-Factor Models
      • Factors: interest rate, inflation, GDP, sector
      • Each factor has its own $\beta$ (sensitivity)
  • Asset Allocation — L8/L9
    • Risk-Free Asset (L8)
      • T-Bills: proxy for risk-free rate
      • True risk-free: maturity matched + price-indexed
    • Two-Asset Allocation (L9)
      • $E(r_w) = (1-w)E(r_1) + wE(r_2)$
      • $\sigma^2_p = (1-w)^2\sigma^2_1 + w^2\sigma^2_2 + 2(1-w)w\,\text{Cov}$
      • $\text{Cov}(r_1,r_2) = \rho\cdot\sigma_1\cdot\sigma_2$
    • Feasible Set
      • $\rho=+1$: straight line (no diversification benefit)
      • $\rho=-1$: zero-risk portfolio possible
      • Optimal: highest utility on efficient frontier

Relative Valuation (Pricing)

  • Philosophy of Relative Valuation
    • Core Assumption
      • Markets are correct on average
      • Can identify relative mispricing within sectors
      • Pricing errors easier to spot & exploit
    • When to Use
      • ✅ Large number of comparable assets available
      • ✅ Assets are actively traded in markets
      • ✅ Common variables exist to standardize prices
      • ✅ Short time horizons (trading/M&A)
      • ❌ Avoid when entire sector is mispriced
    • Wall Street Reality
      • 85% of equity research uses multiples
      • 50%+ of M&A deals priced using multiples
      • Case: IPO Pricing in China (23 P/E ceiling)
  • Key Multiples (倍数)
    • Equity Multiples
      • P/E Ratio (Price/Earnings)
        • Formula: $\frac{\text{Price per Share}}{\text{EPS}}$
        • Trailing P/E: Uses last 12 months (LTM) earnings
        • Forward P/E: Uses estimated future earnings
        • Trap: Affected by capital structure & accounting
      • P/B Ratio (Price/Book)
        • Formula: $\frac{\text{Market Cap}}{\text{Book Value of Equity}}$
        • Best for: Banks, asset-heavy industries
        • Limitation: Book value can be distorted
      • PEG Ratio
        • Formula: $\frac{\text{P/E}}{\text{Growth Rate}}$
        • Adjusts P/E for growth differences
        • Lower PEG = Better value
    • Enterprise Multiples
      • Enterprise Value (EV)
        • Formula: $\text{Market Cap} + \text{Debt} - \text{Cash}$
        • Full Formula: + Preferred + NCI - Associates
        • Represents takeover price
      • EV/EBITDA
        • Most popular M&A multiple
        • ✅ Neutral to capital structure
        • ✅ Excludes D&A (accounting policies)
        • Best for comparing leveraged companies
      • EV/EBIT
        • Similar to EV/EBITDA but includes D&A
        • Better for capital-intensive industries
      • EV/Sales (Revenue Multiple)
        • Useful when EBITDA is negative
        • Common for startups & tech companies
        • Trap: Ignores profitability entirely
  • Implementation Process
    • Step 1: Select Comparables
      • Criteria: Same industry, similar size, growth, risk
      • Methods: Industry peers, precedent transactions
      • Trap: Using dissimilar companies (startup vs mature)
    • Step 2: Calculate Multiples
      • Use consistent definitions (LTM data preferred)
      • Verify data quality & comparability
    • Step 3: Benchmarking
      • Calculate mean, median, range
      • Investigate outliers
      • Adjust for synergies if applicable
    • Step 4: Apply to Target
      • Multiply target's fundamental by selected multiple
      • Establish valuation range (not point estimate)
  • ⭐ Comparable Company Selection (可比公司筛选)
    • Industry Classification
      • GICS (Global Industry Classification Standard)
      • SIC (Standard Industrial Classification)
      • NAICS (North American Industry Classification)
      • Trap: Same industry ≠ comparable business model
    • Size Matching
      • Market Capitalization (±50% range)
      • Revenue/Sales (similar scale)
      • Total Assets (for asset-heavy industries)
      • Why: Size affects growth potential & risk profile
    • Growth Stage
      • Mature: Stable cash flows, low growth
      • Growth: High reinvestment, expanding margins
      • Decline: Shrinking markets, asset liquidation
      • Trap: Comparing growth stock to mature stock
    • Profitability Metrics
      • ROE (Return on Equity): 15-25% typical
      • Operating Margin: Industry-specific benchmarks
      • ROIC (Return on Invested Capital)
      • Why: Profitability drives valuation multiples
    • Geographic Exposure
      • Domestic vs International revenue mix
      • Emerging markets exposure (higher risk)
      • Currency risk considerations
  • ⭐ Multiple Analysis Methods (倍数分析方法)
    • Regression Analysis
      • P/E Regression: $P/E = f(\beta, \text{payout}, g, \sigma)$
      • Formula: $P/E = 16.16 - 7.94\beta + 154.40g - 0.1116\sigma$
      • Key Drivers: Beta (risk), Growth, Payout, Volatility
      • Use: Predict "fair" P/E based on fundamentals
      • Residual Analysis: Identify over/undervalued stocks
    • Distribution Analysis
      • Median: Less affected by outliers than mean
      • Quartiles: Q1 (25%), Q2 (50%), Q3 (75%)
      • Percentile Ranking: Where does target fall?
      • IQR (Interquartile Range): Detect outliers
      • Example: Industry P/E: 10th %ile=12, Median=18, 90th %ile=25
    • Time Series Analysis
      • Historical Multiple Trends (5-10 years)
      • Historical Mean/Median as benchmark
      • Identify cyclical patterns (boom/bust)
      • Mean Reversion: Multiples tend to normalize
      • Trap: Structural changes invalidate historical norms
    • Sensitivity Analysis
      • Tornado Diagram: Rank variable impacts
      • Scenario Analysis: Bull/Base/Bear cases
      • Valuation Range: Min/Max based on assumptions
  • ⭐ Accounting Adjustments (会计调整)
    • EBITDA Standardization
      • Formula: $\text{EBITDA} = \text{EBIT} + \text{D\&A}$
      • Add back: Non-cash charges (stock comp, impairments)
      • Remove: One-time gains (asset sales, litigation)
      • Goal: Normalize to recurring operating performance
    • One-Time Items Removal
      • Restructuring charges (layoffs, plant closures)
      • Asset impairments (goodwill write-downs)
      • Litigation settlements
      • Extraordinary gains (insurance proceeds, asset sales)
      • Trap: "One-time" charges that recur annually
    • LTM/TTM Data Updates
      • LTM: Last Twelve Months (most recent data)
      • TTM: Trailing Twelve Months (same as LTM)
      • Why: More current than annual reports
      • Calculation: Q1+Q2+Q3+Q4 (rolling quarters)
      • Adjust for seasonality if needed
    • Capital Structure Normalization
      • Adjust for excess debt or cash
      • Operating leases → Debt equivalents
      • Pension liabilities adjustments
      • Minority interests (NCI) treatment
  • Special Topics
    • Accounting Considerations
      • EBITDA = EBIT + Depreciation + Amortization
      • Net Income = EBIT - Interest - Tax - NCI - Pref. Div
      • ROE vs ROA definitions
    • Precedent Transactions
      • Use M&A transaction multiples
      • Usually higher than trading multiples (control premium)
      • Challenge: Finding truly comparable deals
    • Adjustments
      • Synergy adjustments for M&A
      • Liquidity discounts for private companies
      • Control premiums
  • Advantages vs Disadvantages
    • Advantages ✅
      • Quick & easy to calculate
      • Market-based, reflects real transactions
      • Easy to communicate & understand
      • Useful for "sanity check" on DCF
    • Disadvantages ❌
      • Can perpetuate market mistakes
      • Cannot detect sector-wide bubbles
      • Requires truly comparable companies
      • Sensitive to market conditions
      • May ignore fundamental differences

Applied Case Analysis

Real Case
Case 1: Consolidated Edison (Valuation)
Data: EPS \$3.17, DPS $2.32. Beta = 0.8.
10Y Bond Rate = 4.1%, Market Premium = 4.5%. ROE = 7.7%.
Task: Calculate Intrinsic Value using Gordon Growth Model.
$$ r_e = R_f + \beta(R_m - R_f) = 4.1\% + 0.8(4.5\%) = 7.7\% $$
Retention Ratio $b = 1 - \frac{2.32}{3.17} = 26.8\%$
$$ g = b \times ROE = 26.8\% \times 7.7\% = 2.06\% $$
$$ P_0 = \frac{D_0(1+g)}{r-g} = \frac{2.32(1.0206)}{0.077 - 0.0206} \approx \$41.98 $$
Real Case
Case 2: ABN AMRO Bank (Two-Stage Valuation)
Background: The largest bank in the Netherlands, Total Assets ~€600 billion.
Data (December 2003): EPS €1.85, DPS €0.90, Beta = 0.95, ROE = 16%
Risk-free rate = 4.35%, Market premium = 4%
Task: Value using Two-Stage Model due to high ROE > k.
Cost of Equity: $$ r_e = R_f + \beta(R_m - R_f) = 4.35\% + 0.95(4\%) = 8.15\% $$ Stage 1 (High Growth): $$ b = 1 - \frac{DPS}{EPS} = 1 - \frac{0.90}{1.85} = 51.35\% $$ $$ g_1 = b \times ROE = 51.35\% \times 16\% = 8.22\% $$ Stage 2 (Stable Growth): $$ g_2 = 4\% \quad \text{(Assumed to match long-term GDP growth)} $$ $$ k_2 = 4.35\% + 1.0(4\%) = 8.35\% \quad \text{(Beta normalizes to 1)} $$ 💡 Key Insight: When ROE (16%) > k (8.15%), the company creates value by retaining earnings!
Assuming 5-year high-growth period: $$ D_1 = 0.90 \times 1.0822 = 0.974 $$ $$ D_2 = 0.974 \times 1.0822 = 1.054 $$ $$ D_3 = 1.054 \times 1.0822 = 1.141 $$ $$ D_4 = 1.141 \times 1.0822 = 1.234 $$ $$ D_5 = 1.234 \times 1.0822 = 1.336 $$
At Year 5, transition to stable growth. Need to adjust payout ratio: $$ \textit{Stable Payout} = 1 - \frac{g_2}{ROE_{stable}} = 1 - \frac{4\%}{8.35\%} = 52.1\% $$ $$ EPS_6 = 1.85 \times (1.0822)^5 \times 1.04 = 2.86 $$ $$ D_6 = 2.86 \times 0.521 = 1.49 $$ Terminal Value: $$ P_5 = \frac{D_6}{k_2 - g_2} = \frac{1.49}{0.0835 - 0.04} = 34.20 $$ (€34.20)
Discount all cash flows back to present: $$ PV(Dividends) = \sum_{t=1}^{5} \frac{D_t}{(1.0815)^t} \approx 4.65 $$ (€4.65) $$ PV(P_5) = \frac{34.20}{(1.0815)^5} = 22.97 $$ (€22.97) Intrinsic Value: $$ V_0 = 4.65 + 22.97 = 27.62 $$ (€27.62)
🎯 Real Outcome:
• December 2003 market price: €18.55 (Undervalued!)
• End of 2007: RBS offered €38.5 to acquire ABN AMRO
• Model predicted upside of ~49% → Actual gain was ~108%!
💡 Lesson: High-ROE companies with moderate payout ratios can be significantly undervalued by the market.
Real Case
Case 3: Zhong Lian Heavy Industry (DuPont Breakdown)
Background: World's 5th largest construction machinery manufacturer.
Problem: Stock price dropped from ¥15 (2011) → ¥9 (2013). Why?
Task: Use DuPont Analysis to diagnose the problem.
$$ \text{ROE}_{2011} = 25.02\% \quad \to \quad \text{ROE}_{2013} = 9.43\% $$ ROE dropped by 62%! But why? Let's decompose: $$ ROE = \underbrace{\text{Net Margin}}_{\text{Profitability}} \times \underbrace{\text{Asset Turnover}}_{\text{Efficiency}} \times \underbrace{\text{Equity Multiplier}}_{\text{Leverage}} $$
$$ \text{Net Margin} = \frac{\text{Net Income}}{\text{Sales}} $$ 2011: $$ \frac{¥8.17B}{¥46.32B} = 18.08\% $$ 2013: $$ \frac{¥3.95B}{¥38.54B} = 10.25\% $$ ❌ Net margin dropped 43%
Reason: Sales fell, but costs remained sticky. Competition intensified!
• 2011 Costs: ¥36.6B
• 2013 Costs: ¥33.0B (only 10% reduction while sales fell 17%)
$$ \text{Asset Turnover} = \frac{\text{Sales}}{\text{Total Assets}} $$ 2011: $0.69$ → 2013: $0.43$ ❌ Efficiency dropped 38%
Reason: Sales decreased, but assets increased (especially accounts receivable)
💡 Warning sign: Company gave customers longer payment terms to maintain sales!
$$ \text{Equity Multiplier} = \frac{\text{Total Assets}}{\text{Total Equity}} $$ 2011: $2.01$ → 2013: $2.14$ ⚠️ Leverage increased 6.5%
Implication: Company took on more debt to compensate for falling profitability.
🔍 Full DuPont Analysis:
2011: ROE = $18.08\% \times 0.69 \times 2.01 = 25.02\%$
2013: ROE = $10.25\% \times 0.43 \times 2.14 = 9.43\%$
💡 Key Lessons:
1. ❌ Margin compression + efficiency decline = value destruction
2. ⚠️ Increasing leverage during downturn amplifies risk
3. 🚩 Rising A/R (accounts receivable) is a red flag
4. 📉 Stock price correctly reflected deteriorating fundamentals
Advanced
Case 4: S&P 500 Index Valuation (Crisis Period)
Context: January 2009, during the Financial Crisis.
Data: LTM Dividend =\$$28.05$, Expected $g_1$ = 4% (5 years), $g_2$ = 2.21%
Risk-free rate = 2.21%, Market risk premium = 6% (elevated due to crisis)
Challenge: Is the index undervalued at 903?
For the market index, $\beta = 1$ by definition. $$ k = R_f + \beta \times \text{Risk Premium} = 2.21\% + 1.0 \times 6\% = 8.21\% $$ 💡 Note: Risk premium is elevated (6% vs normal 4-5%) due to crisis conditions.
Stage 1 Dividends (g = 4%): $$ D_1 = 28.05 \times 1.04 = 29.17 $$ $$ \vdots $$ $$ D_5 = 28.05 \times (1.04)^5 = 34.12 $$ $$ PV(\text{Stage 1}) = \sum_{t=1}^{5} \frac{D_t}{(1.0821)^t} \approx 124.71 $$ Terminal Value: $$ P_5 = \frac{D_6}{k - g_2} = \frac{34.12 \times 1.0221}{0.0821 - 0.0221} = \frac{34.87}{0.06} = 581.17 $$ $$ PV(P_5) = \frac{581.17}{(1.0821)^5} = 387.75 $$
Intrinsic Value: $$ V_0 = 124.71 + 387.75 = \mathbf{512.46} $$ Actual Price: 903 ❓ Paradox! The model says 512, but the market is at 903?
💡 Possible Explanations:
1. Dividend growth assumptions too pessimistic (crisis mentality)
2. Risk premium of 6% may be temporarily elevated
3. Market pricing in a quicker recovery
4. Dividends alone understate total shareholder returns (buybacks not included)
🎯 Lesson: During crises, valuation models can diverge significantly from prices. The "right" answer depends heavily on assumptions about recovery speed and risk appetite.
Philosophy
Case 5: John Bogle's Index Fund Revolution
Background: Founder of Vanguard, creator of first index fund.
Philosophy: Most active managers cannot beat the market after fees.
Question: How much does fee difference matter over time?
Scenario: Two investors, 50-year horizon, market return = 7%
• Investor A: Active fund (2% annual fee) → Net return = 5%
• Investor B: Index fund (0.05% fee) → Net return = 6.95%
Starting with $1: Active Fund (5% net): $$ FV = 1 \times (1.05)^{50} = \$11.47 $$ Index Fund (6.95% net): $$ FV = 1 \times (1.0695)^{50} = \$29.46 $$
🎯 Result: Index investor has 2.6x more wealth!
Lost to fees: $\$29.46 - \$11.47 = \$17.99$ (61% of potential wealth!) 💡 "If a statue is ever erected to honor the person who has done the most for American investors, the hands-down choice should be John Bogle." — Warren Buffett
Vanguard Today:
• Assets under management: $5 trillion+
• Passive funds: 33% of U.S. market share
Industry Shift:
• Active fund fees have dropped from 2% → ~1%
• Index funds force discipline and cost awareness
• Democratized investing for retail investors
💡 Lesson for Valuation:
Even small differences in assumptions (like fees) compound dramatically over time. This applies equally to growth rates, discount rates, and terminal values in DCF models.
Gordon Model
Case 6: American Electric Power (Stable Utility)
Data (2008): DPS = $1.64, Historical growth = 3.3%, Beta = 0.62
Risk-free rate = 3.32%, Market premium = 5%
Market Price (Sept 2009): $31.06
Task: Apply Gordon Model and compare.
Step 1: Cost of Equity $$ r_e = 3.32\% + 0.62 \times 5\% = 6.42\% $$ 💡 Beta = 0.62 indicates a defensive stock (typical for utilities). Step 2: Gordon Model $$ P_0 = \frac{D_0(1+g)}{r-g} = \frac{1.64 \times 1.033}{0.0642 - 0.033} = \frac{1.694}{0.0312} = \$54.30 $$
Comparison:
• Intrinsic Value: $54.30
• Market Price: $31.06
• Upside: +75% 💡 Why the discount?
• 2009 was post-financial crisis → elevated risk aversion
• Utilities were sold off with broader market
• Perfect candidate for value investors using DDM
Relative Valuation
Case 7: Coca-Cola vs Pepsi (P/E Multiple Comparison)
Background: Two beverage giants with similar business models.
Data (2023):
• Coca-Cola: P/E = 25.3, β = 0.62, ROE = 42.8%, Payout = 75%, g = 5%
• PepsiCo: P/E = 22.1, β = 0.68, ROE = 48.2%, Payout = 65%, g = 6%
Risk-free rate = 4.5%, Market premium = 5.5%
Question: Which company is relatively undervalued?
Using the P/E regression formula from Lecture 5: $$ P/E = 16.16 - 7.94\beta + 154.40g - 0.1116\sigma + \text{payout adjustment} $$ Coca-Cola: $$ \text{Theoretical P/E} = 16.16 - 7.94(0.62) + 154.40(0.05) - 0.1116(20) $$ $$ = 16.16 - 4.92 + 7.72 - 2.23 = 16.73 $$ PepsiCo: $$ \text{Theoretical P/E} = 16.16 - 7.94(0.68) + 154.40(0.06) - 0.1116(22) $$ $$ = 16.16 - 5.40 + 9.26 - 2.46 = 17.56 $$ 💡 Note: Assumed σ (volatility) = 20% for Coke, 22% for Pepsi based on historical data.
Company Actual P/E Theoretical P/E Premium/Discount
Coca-Cola 25.3 16.73 +51.2%
PepsiCo 22.1 17.56 +25.9%
Interpretation:
• Both companies trade at a premium to their theoretical P/E
• Coca-Cola's premium (51%) is twice that of PepsiCo (26%)
• PepsiCo appears relatively undervalued compared to Coca-Cola
Why does Coca-Cola command a higher premium? 1. Brand Power (Intangible Asset)
• Coca-Cola brand value: $97.9B (Interbrand 2023)
• Pepsi brand value: $18.2B
• 🎯 Coke's brand is 5.4x stronger 2. Geographic Diversification
• Coca-Cola: 200+ countries, 50% revenue from emerging markets
• PepsiCo: More U.S.-centric (60% North America) 3. Product Focus
• Coca-Cola: Pure beverage play (100% beverages)
• PepsiCo: 55% beverages, 45% snacks (Frito-Lay)
• 💡 Investors pay premium for "pure play" exposure 4. Historical Performance
• Coca-Cola: 130+ years of dividend payments
• Consistent execution, less volatility
💡 Key Insight: The regression model captures quantitative factors (β, g, payout), but premiums often reflect qualitative factors (brand, moat, management quality).
Scenario Analysis: Bull Case for PepsiCo:
✅ Trading at lower premium (26% vs 51%)
✅ Higher ROE (48.2% vs 42.8%)
✅ Higher growth rate (6% vs 5%)
✅ Diversification (snacks buffer beverage headwinds)
Bull Case for Coca-Cola:
✅ Stronger brand moat
✅ Better emerging market exposure
✅ Lower beta (0.62 vs 0.68) = less risky
✅ Pure beverage play (simpler business model)
🎯 Recommendation:
• Value investors: PepsiCo (lower premium, higher ROE/growth)
• Quality investors: Coca-Cola (brand moat, defensive characteristics)
• Pair trade: Long PepsiCo, Short Coca-Cola (bet on premium convergence)
💡 Lessons for Relative Valuation:
1. ⚠️ Never use P/E in isolation — always compare to fundamentals
2. 📊 Regression models provide baseline, qualitative factors explain premiums
3. 🔍 "Expensive" vs "Overvalued" are different — Coke may justify its premium
4. 🎯 Relative valuation works best for comparable companies in same industry

Interactive Financial Lab

Visually explore how variables affect value. "Don't just calculate it, feel it."

📖 What is this model?

The Intuition: Imagine a machine (the company) that prints money (dividends) for you forever. The Gordon Growth Model calculates how much you should pay for that machine today.

It assumes the money-printing speed accelerates by $g$ every year. The price depends on how impatient or risk-averse you are ($k$).

Start Here: Think of a utility company like Consolidated Edison. It pays a steady dividend that grows slightly with inflation.

Explore how fundamental factors drive P/E multiples

Systematic risk - lower β → higher P/E

Expected earnings growth - strongest P/E driver

Dividend payout - higher payout → slight P/E boost

Earnings volatility - higher σ → lower P/E

📐 Regression Formula:
P/E = 16.16 - 7.94β + 154.40g - 0.1116σ + payout adj.
